- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥ 0.5) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- When sentiment is negative (≤ -0.3) or volatile, model often underestimates downside risk; add buffer below forecast or anticipate sharper declines.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model frequently overcorrects and forecasts a prolonged flat or downward trend — adjust for mean reversion with a lagged decay factor.
- If sentiment is flat (0.0–0.3) and price history shows strong mean reversion, model often fails to recognize reversion — apply a smoothing filter or use recent 7-day average as anchor.
- For 30-day forecasts, model often overestimates early in the horizon (first 5–7 days) when sentiment is bullish — reduce initial forecast by 2–5% to account for momentum decay.
- When sentiment history shows repeated reversals (e.g., +0.8 → -0.2 → +0.6), model tends to misread trend direction — use sentiment volatility as a signal to adjust forecast directionality.
